title: Functions, Polynomials, and Rational Equations
lead: Function notation looks intimidating, but a function is a machine that takes an input and gives an output. On the Digital SAT these questions are rarely abstract. They are about interpreting what the machine does in a real-world context.

parts.title: Part 1 · The core idea
parts.html:
The notation f(x) is a name for a rule.

  • f is the name of the rule.
  • x is the input, what you put in.
  • f(x) is the output, what the rule gives back.

f(3) = 10 says: when the input is 3, the rule gives back 10. On a graph, that is the point (3, 10).

parts.title: Part 2 · Evaluation and interpretation
parts.html:
1. Evaluation. Replace every x with the input.

If f(x)=2x2+5, what is f(4)? f(4)=2(4)2+5=2(16)+5=37

2. Interpretation, the most common type.

The function P(t)=500(1.05)t models the population after t years. What does P(10) represent? The population after 10 years.

Always check the labels. If t is in years, 10 means 10 years. If P is in thousands, the result is in thousands.

3. Reading a graph. On a graph of y = f(x), f(a) is the y-value where x = a. To find f(2), find x = 2 on the horizontal axis, move up or down to the curve, and read the y-value.

The reverse question, “for what value of x is f(x) = 2?”, starts from the vertical axis: find y = 2, move across to the curve, and read the x-value.

Tip. On a function question with a long word problem, look at the function before the text. What is the input, and what is the output? Write them down: if x is time, f(x) is amount. That mapping often answers the question before you finish the paragraph.

parts.title: Part 3 · Composite functions
parts.html:
A composite function is f(g(x)). It means: do g first, then put that result into f.

f(x)=x+2 and g(x)=3x. What is f(g(2))? Inside first: g(2)=3(2)=6
Then: f(6)=6+2=8

On the SAT these are often hidden in tables.

xf(x)g(x)
175
391
5123

What is f(g(1))? Find g(1) in the table: 5. Then find f(5): 12. The answer is 12. The trap answer is 7, which is f(1).

parts.title: Part 4 · Domain and range
parts.html:
• Domain: the set of all possible inputs (x-values). In context this is often “time cannot be negative”, so x ≥ 0.
  • Range: the set of all possible outputs (y-values). In context this is often “the population cannot be negative”, so f(x) ≥ 0.

If a model is f(t) = 100(0.8)t, where t is the number of years since 2000, and it is now 2025, the domain is 0 ≤ t ≤ 25.

parts.title: Part 5 · Function transformations
parts.html:
A transformation changes the position or shape of the graph of y = f(x) without changing its basic structure.

ChangeEffect on the graph
f(x − h)Shifts right by h
f(x + h)Shifts left by h
f(x) + kShifts up by k
f(x) − kShifts down by k
−f(x)Reflects over the x-axis

The horizontal shift is counter-intuitive: x − 3 moves the graph to the right. A change inside the brackets acts on x and goes the opposite way to its sign. A change outside acts on y and goes the way it looks.

g(x)=f(x−3)+2 The whole graph moves right 3 and up 2
If (1,4) is on the graph of f, then (4,6) is on the graph of g
If f(x)=x2, then g(x)=(x−3)2+2, with vertex (3,2)

This is why vertex form from Class 9 works: a(x − h)² + k is the parabola ax² shifted right h and up k.

Desmos tip. Define f(x) first, then type y=f(x-3)+2 on a new line to see the shift. Use sliders for h and k in y=f(x-h)+k to watch the graph move.

parts.title: Part 6 · Polynomial graphs and zeros
parts.html:
What counts as a polynomial. A polynomial is a sum of terms of the form axn, where every exponent is a whole number (0, 1, 2, 3, …). 4x³ − x + 6, x² − 25 and the constant 9 are all polynomials. 1/x, x⁻² and √x are not, because their exponents are negative or fractional.

A polynomial function accepts every real number as an input, and its graph is one unbroken curve with no gaps and no vertical asymptotes. The degree is the largest exponent.

Two forms, two jobs. Neither is better; the question decides.

FormExampleUse it for
Factored(x − 3)(x + 4)Zeros and x-intercepts: 3 and −4
Expandedx² + x − 12Comparing coefficients, adding and subtracting, the y-intercept (−12)

Beyond quadratics, polynomials have more turns and more zeros (x-intercepts). Three facts answer most questions.

  • Zeros. If (x − a) is a factor, then a is a zero: the graph meets the x-axis at x = a. It works in reverse too: an x-intercept at 4 means (x − 4) is a factor.
  • Multiplicity. If a factor is squared, like (x − a)², the graph touches the x-axis at a and turns back without crossing.
  • End behavior. Even-degree polynomials (x², x⁴) go the same direction at both ends. Odd-degree polynomials (x³, x⁵) go opposite directions. With a positive leading coefficient the right end goes up; with a negative one it goes down.
f(x)=(x−2)2(x+1) Zeros: x=2 and x=−1
At x=−1 the graph crosses the axis; at x=2 it touches and turns back
Degree 3, positive leading coefficient → left end down, right end up
y-intercept: f(0)=(−2)2(1)=4

Common mistake. The sign flips between factor and zero, as in Class 9. The factor (x + 1) gives the zero −1, not 1.

parts.title: Part 7 · Rational functions
parts.html:
A rational expression is a fraction with a polynomial on top and a polynomial underneath, such as (x + 1) / (x − 5). It is one polynomial divided by another. The quickest way to tell a rational function from a polynomial is to look for a variable in a denominator.

Polynomial functionRational function
FormP(x)P(x) / Q(x)
DomainAll real numbersAll real numbers except those that make the denominator zero
GraphOne unbroken curveMay have holes or vertical asymptotes
ZerosWhere the polynomial equals zeroWhere the numerator equals zero, if that input is allowed

Excluded values. Division by zero is undefined, so any input that makes the denominator zero is not in the domain. Set the denominator equal to zero to find it.

f(x)=x+1x−5 Denominator zero: x−5=0 → x=5 is excluded
The factor does not cancel → vertical asymptote at x=5
Zero: numerator x+1=0 → x=−1, which is allowed

Not every rational function has an excluded value. In 3 / (x² + 4) the denominator is at least 4 for every real x, so the domain is all real numbers. What makes a function rational is the fraction, not the asymptote.

Cancelling does not restore the domain. This is the main point of confusion in the topic.

h(x)=x2−4x−2 Restriction first: x−2=0 → x≠2
Factor: (x−2)(x+2)x−2
Cancel: h(x)=x+2, for x≠2

The graph of h is the line y = x + 2 with a hole at (2, 4). It is not the same function as g(x) = x + 2, whose domain includes 2. The simplified form is equal to the original only where the original was defined.

The denominator factor…The graph has…
cancels with a factor in the numeratora hole at that x-value
stays after simplifyinga vertical asymptote at that x-value

Common mistake. Counting a cancelled value as a zero. In h above, the numerator is zero at x = 2 and at x = −2. Only −2 is an x-intercept. At 2 there is a hole.

The order of work

  1. Look at the original expression. A variable in a denominator means rational.
  2. Find the restrictions first. Set every original denominator equal to zero and write down the excluded values, before cancelling anything.
  3. Factor and simplify. Cancelled factors give holes; remaining denominator factors give asymptotes.
  4. Match the form to the question. Factored form for zeros and restrictions, expanded form for coefficients, a graph when a picture is quickest.
  5. Check every candidate answer against the restrictions from step 2.

parts.title: Part 8 · Operations with rational expressions
parts.html:
Rational expressions follow the same rules as ordinary fractions. The only new skill is factoring, because the things you cancel are now polynomials.

Simplifying. 6/15 simplifies to 2/5 because 3 is a factor of both numbers. A rational expression simplifies the same way: factor the top and the bottom, then cancel any factor they share.

3x+6x2+2x Factor: 3(x+2)x(x+2)
Cancel (x+2): 3x

Common mistake. Cancelling terms. Only factors cancel, meaning things that are multiplied. In (x + 6) / (x + 2) the x's cannot be cancelled, because they are added, not multiplied. If nothing factors, nothing cancels.

Multiplying and dividing

OperationRule
Multiplya/b × c/d = ac / bd
Dividea/b ÷ c/d = a/b × d/c = ad / bc (multiply by the reciprocal)
  1. Factor every numerator and denominator.
  2. Cancel any factor that appears on both a top and a bottom.
  3. Multiply what is left, top by top and bottom by bottom.

Cancel before multiplying. Multiplying first produces long polynomials that then have to be factored again.

x2−9x+1×x+1x−3 Factor: (x−3)(x+3)x+1×x+1x−3
Cancel (x+1) and (x−3): x+3
x+4x−1÷x+42x Flip the second fraction: x+4x−1×2xx+4
Cancel (x+4): 2xx−1

Adding and subtracting. Numerators can be added or subtracted only when the denominators are the same.

Rule for unlike denominators
a/b ± c/d = (ad ± bc) / bd
  1. Find a common denominator. The product of the two denominators almost always works.
  2. Rewrite each fraction with that denominator.
  3. Add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator.
  4. Combine like terms.
  5. Factor and cancel if possible.
Same denominator. x2x+2+5x+6x+2 Add the numerators: x2+5x+6x+2
Factor: (x+2)(x+3)x+2
Cancel: x+3
Different denominators. 2x+1+3x−2 Common denominator: (x+1)(x−2)
Numerator: 2(x−2)+3(x+1)=2x−4+3x+3=5x−1
Result: 5x−1(x+1)(x−2)

Subtraction trap. When subtracting, put the second numerator in brackets so the minus sign reaches every term: 5 − (x − 2) is 7 − x, not 3 − x.

On the SAT the numerators and denominators are often quadratics, so the factoring from Class 9 is what makes these questions quick.

parts.title: Part 9 · Rational equations
parts.html:
A rational equation has a variable in a denominator. The simplest form is P(x) / Q(x) = 0.

  • The rule. A fraction is zero only if the numerator is zero and the denominator is not.
  • Extraneous solutions. Check whether each solution makes a denominator zero. If it does, discard it.
x2−9x−3=0 Numerator zero: x2−9=0 → x=3 or x=−3
x=3 makes the denominator zero → discard
Answer: x=−3

When the equation has fractions on both sides, multiply every term by the denominators to clear them, solve, and run the same check.

6x−1=3 Multiply by (x−1): 6=3(x−1) → x=3
Check: the denominator is 3−1=2, not zero → x=3

Multiplying by the denominator turns the equation into a polynomial equation, which is easier to solve but has forgotten the restriction. The check is what brings it back.

xx−2=2x−2+3 Restriction: x≠2
Multiply by (x−2): x=2+3(x−2) → x=3x−4 → x=2
x=2 is excluded → the equation has no solution

parts.title: Part 10 · The Desmos angle
parts.html:
• Polynomial zeros: type the polynomial and click the x-intercepts. A point where the curve touches the axis and turns back is a repeated zero.
  • Rational equations: graph the left side and the right side as two expressions and read the x-coordinates of the intersections. A value that makes a denominator zero shows as a gap or a vertical break, never as an intersection.
  • Holes are easy to miss. Desmos draws a hole as a tiny gap or not at all, so the graph of (x² − 4) / (x − 2) looks like a complete line. Find excluded values from the equation, and use the graph only to confirm.
  • Function values: define f(x)=2x^2+5, then type f(4). Composite functions work the same way: f(g(2)).
